opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot. One thing I'd say up front is that we're a pretty small organization, so the question for us is less "what's the most important problem in AI safety" and more "what's the most important problem where we in particular have a comparative advantage."

A few things I think we're relatively good at. First, we've spent a lot of time thinking carefully about threat models, specifically the scenario where you have AI systems that are quite capable and might be actively trying to subvert your safety measures. A lot of the field historically has focused on making models not want to do bad things, which is great and important, but we've leaned into the complementary question: suppose you fail at that, or you can't tell whether you've succeeded. How do you still deploy these systems and get useful work out of them without catastrophe? That's the AI control agenda, and I think we've built up a decent amount of conceptual clarity there that's somewhat rare.

Second, we're reasonably good at taking fuzzy, high-level safety concerns and turning them into concrete, empirical research setups: here's a red team, here's a blue team, here's what counts as winning, here's how you measure it. That methodology turns out to be pretty transferable, and I think it's one of the more useful things we've contributed, honestly maybe more useful than any particular result.

Third, because we're independent, we can say things and pursue directions that might be awkward for people inside AI companies. We can be somewhat blunt about how prepared or unprepared the labs are, and we can work on stuff that's useful across many developers rather than tied to one company's roadmap.

So how does that shape where we're going? I expect we'll keep pushing on control, but with more emphasis on making it practical: working with people at labs to figure out what protocols they'd actually implement, what the costs are, and where the hard cases are. And I think increasingly we'll be thinking about the messier, more realistic settings, like agents doing long autonomous tasks, models with access to sensitive infrastructure, and research sabotage, where the clean toy settings we started with don't capture everything.

The other thing I'd flag is that a lot of our value might come from strategy and field-building work: helping people think clearly about which safety measures actually buy you the most risk reduction per unit of effort, given that the labs are probably going to be in a big hurry. I think having a clear picture of "here's what a reasonably cautious developer would do in a rushed world" is really valuable, and we're well placed to help articulate it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest way to describe Redwood's strengths is that we're pretty good at taking a vague, scary-sounding concern about AI and turning it into a concrete, empirical research question that you can actually make progress on in a few months. That's what we did with adversarial training back in the day, and it's what the control agenda is now. The question of "what if the model is scheming against you?" sounds like science fiction, but you can reformulate it as: suppose the model is actively trying to subvert your safety measures, what's the best protocol the lab can run, and how well does it hold up when a red team plays the untrusted model? That's a well-defined game. You can run it. You can get numbers.

So I think that pushes us in a few directions. One is that we'll keep doing this kind of work where we build out the control framework: more realistic settings, more sophisticated attack policies, more careful thinking about what the deployment actually looks like, so that when labs are deploying models that are capable enough to be dangerous, there's an existing body of techniques and evaluations they can just pick up.

The second thing is that we're pretty comfortable being conceptual when it's useful. A lot of the value we've added isn't a particular experiment, it's the argument for why you should be thinking about safety from the perspective of "the model might be adversarial" at all, and what that implies about which techniques actually give you guarantees versus which ones just make you feel better. I expect we'll keep spending a lot of time writing things up that are basically "here is how to think about this problem", because that seems to have been unusually influential relative to the effort.

And the third thing, which is maybe a weakness as much as a strength, is that we're small and we don't train frontier models. So we can't do the kind of research that requires enormous compute or access to internals of the biggest systems. What we can do is be the people who think really hard about how the labs should be using the tools they have, and then work with people at the labs to actually get those things implemented. I think a lot of our future is being a sort of external research partner to the places that are actually going to be deploying these systems, rather than trying to compete with them on the science of building the models themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think the way I’d frame it is that we should look for research directions where our particular strengths make a difference, rather than trying to cover every important problem in AI safety.

For me, that means putting a lot of weight on making questions concrete: can we turn a concern about how an AI system might behave into an experiment, try some ways of addressing it, and learn something that changes what we’d recommend people do?

But I wouldn’t want us to get too attached to a particular agenda just because it fits what we’re already good at. There’s a balance between exploiting your strengths and asking whether the work is actually answering the most important questions. I’d want our future direction to be driven by that combination.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it as a question of where we can make the most useful contribution. There are lots of important problems in AI safety, but that doesn’t mean Redwood should work on all of them. We should choose problems where our strengths let us make progress and where that progress would actually change something about how people build or deploy AI.

And I think that should be an iterative process. You try a research direction, see whether you’re learning things that matter, and update. I’d be reluctant to commit to a very detailed long-term agenda just because it sounds compelling in advance.
